titre: Prototype-Guided Test-Time Adaptation for Real-Time EMG-Based Gesture Recognition.
auteurs: Ma Yingtong, Wang Yalin, Dai Chenyun, Guo Yao
resume: Surface electromyography (sEMG) signals facilitate intuitive human-machine interaction and are widely employed in applications such as prosthetics and rehabilitation. However, sEMG signal distributions are highly sensitive to variations in electrode placement, user physiology, and session conditions, which significantly hinder model generalization in real-world settings. To address this, we propose EMG-based structure-aware test-time adaptive refinement (EMG-STAR), a test-time adaptation (TTA) framework tailored for online deployment without access to target data during training. EMG-STAR improves model stability by fusing historical and batch-wise normalization statistics from both source and target domains, effectively alleviating domain shifts. Furthermore, it refines predictions using a prototype-assisted feature clustering method that enforces consistency among semantically similar target samples. To further enhance reliability, the framework jointly leverages prediction confidence and distributional alignment to filter out noisy pseudo-labels during adaptation. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on two public datasets, Hyser, and NinaPro-DB2, demonstrate that EMG-STAR consistently outperforms ten existing TTA methods. Interpretability analysis using Grad-CAM reveals that EMG-STAR predominantly attends to physiologically meaningful muscle activation regions, suggesting that the model captures neuromuscular structures rather than transient signal noise.

titre: The Arabic Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (Arabic-COPM) in Pediatric Rehabilitation: Quantitative Reliability Study.
auteurs: Hadoush Hikmat, Sweileh Rawan, Almasri Nihad
resume: The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) has achieved global implementation across 35 countries in more than 20 language versions. However, its psychometric properties for children with physical disabilities remain unverified. This study aimed to evaluate the interrater and test-retest reliability of the Arabic version of the COPM (Arabic-COPM) in this pediatric population. A cross-sectional study was conducted using a convenience sample of parents of children with physical disabilities recruited from multi-rehabilitation centers. For the interrater reliability assessment, 100 parents completed the Arabic-COPM through independent interviews with 2 raters. A subsample of 30 (30%) parents repeated the assessment after a 14-day interval for the test-retest reliability analysis, in which they identified their children's 5 most significant daily activity problems and rated the performance and satisfaction levels for each problem using standardized 10-point scales. Reliability analyses demonstrated excellent psychometric properties. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) for interrater reliability were 0.84 (performance) and 0.80 (satisfaction), while test-retest reliability coefficients were 0.83 and 0.91, respectively. Interrater agreement analysis revealed 73% concordance in problem prioritization between independent assessors. Bland-Altman plots indicated narrow limits of agreement for both performance (-1.69 to 1.60) and satisfaction scores (-1.03 to 0.98). Cohen κ analysis for problem categorization demonstrated slight-to-fair interrater agreement and slight-to-moderate test-retest agreement across COPM domains. Content analysis identified a predominant concern with daily activities (82%-85% of problems), particularly mobility functions, followed by dressing and eating subcategories. The Arabic-COPM demonstrated excellent reliability metrics for both interrater consistency and temporal stability when administered to parents of children with physical disabilities. These robust measurement properties support its application as a validated instrument for implementing family-centered rehabilitation approaches in Arabic-speaking clinical contexts.

titre: Implementation of a Professional Version of the Multiple Errands Test in Vocational Rehabilitation: Can It Complement Traditional Cognitive Assessment After Traumatic Brain Injury and Predict Return to Work?
auteurs: Wicki Gérard, Aubert Christelle, Benaim Charles, Mühl Andréas, Fédou Michel, Vuadens Philippe, Bellmann Anne
revue: The Journal of head trauma rehabilitation
resume: To evaluate the sensitivity and ecological contribution of the Multiple Errands Test in a Professional Setting, a vocationally oriented executive function assessment, after traumatic brain injury (TBI), and explore its association with return to work (RTW). A Swiss neurorehabilitation center with an integrated vocational rehabilitation workshop. Fifty adults with TBI undergoing return-to-work rehabilitation and 40 control participants without brain lesions. Single-center prospective psychometric study with retrospective use of previously collected data. Multiple Errands Test in a Professional Setting error scores, conventional executive and attentional tests, a clinic-adapted Multiple Errands Test, and RTW at 12 months. Participants with TBI made significantly more rule-breaking, inefficiency, partial-realization, interpretation, and judgment errors than controls. Overall, 82% of participants with TBI failed at least one Multiple Errands Test in a Professional Setting measure, including more than 70% who succeeded on conventional executive or attentional assessments. Concordance with traditional assessment was statistically significant for total and attentional assessment but low. Multiple Errands Test in a Professional Setting performance had limited predictive value for RTW, whereas attentional impairment showed a stronger association with work status. Multiple Errands Test in a Professional Setting detects work-relevant executive difficulties often missed by standard tests and may support individualized vocational rehabilitation planning after TBI when interpreted within a broader clinical functional assessment framework.

titre: Field-Based Assessment of Running Biomechanics Using Global Positioning System/Inertial Measurement Unit: Establishing Construct Validity in Elite Athletes.
auteurs: Weber Jason A, Peeling Peter, Hart Nicolas H, Newton Robert U
revue: Journal of strength and conditioning research
resume: Weber, JA, Peeling, P, Hart, NH, and Newton, RU. Field-based assessment of running biomechanics using global positioning system/inertial measurement unit: Establishing construct validity in elite athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To examine the between-session reliability and construct validity of global positioning system (GPS)/inertial measurement unit (IMU)-derived biomechanical variables during field-based running in elite athletes. Fifty-four professional male Australian Football League players completed repeated 40-m runs across 1 competitive season (3,943 trials). Running speed for the 20-40 m segment was quantified via 10-Hz GPS and center-of-mass displacement metrics derived from a 100-Hz IMU. Between-session reliability (n = 25, mean (k) = 2.95) was assessed using a linear mixed-effects model with velocity as a fixed covariate, expressed as intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) (absolute agreement), SEM, and minimal detectable change95, with 95% confidence intervals from athlete-cluster bootstrap. Five candidate models were compared; Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines was selected based on lowest cross-validation root mean squared error (RMSE). Validity was assessed over 100 iterations of athlete-stratified cross-validation (80/20 split), with agreement quantified by ICC, RMSE, and athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis. Velocity-adjusted reliability ranged from moderate to good-to-excellent across 12 variables (ICC = 0.65-0.92), with 8 meeting good-to-excellent thresholds (ICC ≥0.75). Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines accounted for 93% of variance in running speed (R2 = 0.93; RMSE = 0.20 m·s-1; ICC = 0.96 ± 0.004). Athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis indicated negligible bias (-0.01 m·s-1; LoA: -0.243 to +0.223 m·s-1) with no proportional bias (p = 0.369); limits narrowed in athletes with adequate data volume (n = 47; -0.207 to +0.189 m·s-1). Mechanics-speed relationships persisted after accounting for within-athlete clustering (residual between-athlete ICC = 0.43), and the most influential predictors were consistent with established biomechanical determinants of speed. These findings support GPS/IMU-derived biomechanical variables as field-based indicators of running mechanics. Pending replication and criterion validation, this approach may offer practitioners an accessible framework for monitoring performance and rehabilitation.

titre: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Validation of the Yoruba Version of the Barriers to Being Active Quiz in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
auteurs: Oyewole Olufemi O, Bolarinde Olufemi S, Ale Ayotunde O, Ogunlana Michael O, Gurayah Thavanesi, Odole Adesola C
revue: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy
resume: A third of Nigerians with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are physically inactive. Assessing barriers to physical activity (PA) using a culturally sensitive tool is essential for developing strategies to improve PA. Culturally adapted assessment of barriers to PA may contribute to individualised exercise prescription, behavioural interventions, and culturally responsive rehabilitation. The ease of scoring and fewer items than other tools make the Barriers to Being Active Quiz (BBAQ) preferable. This study translated and culturally adapted the BBAQ into Yoruba and validated it among Yoruba-speaking adults with T2DM. The validation study involved translating, culturally adapting, and psychometrically evaluating the BBAQ into Yoruba. Participants completed the short form of the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ-SF) and the BBAQ-Y twice to assess construct validity, internal consistency, and test-retest reliability. The mean age of the 189 participants was 62.06 ± 10.49 years, and the median (IQR) duration of diabetes was 84 (36-144) months. The structural validity of the BBAQ-Y was acceptable after three error modifications. Fit indices were acceptable (CFI = 0.90, TLI = 0.90, RMSEA = 0.07). Convergent validity was partially supported, as a significant inverse correlation was found between the Yoruba IPAQ-SF and the BBAQ-Y (r = -0.216, p = 0.003). Discriminant validity was established, as individuals with low physical activity reported higher barriers than those with moderate or high physical activity (p = 0.001). Cronbach's alpha was excellent (α = 0.893), and test-retest reliability was moderate (ICC = 0.623), whereas the domain ICCs ranged from 0.295 to 0.533. The measurement error indicators of SEM and SDC were 9.01 and 24.97, respectively. The BBAQ-Y possesses adequate construct validity and internal consistency, with moderate test-retest reliability and more modest domain-level reliability and convergent validity, comparable to those of existing versions.

titre: Preliminary psychometric evaluation of the Multidimensional Psychological Flexibility Inventory in adults with spinal cord injury.
auteurs: Kim Minjung, Han Areum, Hong Ickpyo
revue: The journal of spinal cord medicine
resume: Psychological flexibility is a key treatment target in acceptance and commitment therapy and is increasingly relevant to rehabilitation research involving adults with spinal cord injury (SCI). This study examined preliminary psychometric properties of the Multidimensional Psychological Flexibility Inventory-Long Form (MPFI-LF) and Short Form (MPFI-SF) in adults with SCI. Cross-sectional online survey with a two-week test-retest subsample. Community-based online recruitment across the United States. Adults with traumatic or non-traumatic SCI (N = 159; 50.3% female; mean age = 42.2 years). A subset of 59 participants completed the retest assessment. MPFI-LF, MPFI-SF, and other related measures to examine internal consistency, test-retest reliability, subscale intercorrelations, convergent validity, and floor and ceiling effects. The MPFI-LF demonstrated good to excellent internal consistency across composite scores and subscales. The MPFI-SF showed acceptable to good internal consistency for most scores, although the Acceptance subscale showed poor internal consistency. Composite scores and most subscales showed moderate to good test-retest reliability, although several MPFI-SF inflexibility subscales showed poor to moderate stability. Subscale intercorrelations generally supported theoretically expected patterns, although experiential avoidance showed weak associations with other inflexibility subscales. Convergent validity was supported by moderate to strong correlations with related ACT process measures. No floor or ceiling effects were observed. Findings provide preliminary support for the MPFI, particularly the MPFI-LF, as a multidimensional measure of psychological flexibility and inflexibility in adults with SCI. Further research is needed to evaluate factorial validity, discriminant validity, and responsiveness.

titre: Family Caregivers' Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Towards Acute Exacerbations of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease.
auteurs: Zhang Ling, Zhou Quan, Qi Yan, Zhao Jing, Hui Zhifen, Xie Chaochao
resume: To assess knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) among family caregivers of patients with acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD). This cross-sectional survey recruited caregivers through Yizheng People's Hospital and associated community settings in Jiangsu Province, China, from July to September 2024. A self-developed questionnaire was administered online, on paper, or with staff assistance. Associations were examined using Spearman correlations, multivariable logistic regression, and structural equation modeling (SEM). Psychometric properties were additionally evaluated using a six-expert content-relevance assessment and a three-factor measurement model. Among 500 caregivers, 278 (55.6%) were female. Mean knowledge, attitude, and practice scores were 14.07 ± 5.15, 33.08 ± 3.71, and 36.14 ± 4.10, respectively. Using a standardized-score threshold >70%, 231 (46.2%) met the operational knowledge criterion, 401 (80.2%) met the positive-attitude criterion, and 338 (67.6%) met the proactive-practice criterion. Higher knowledge (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 1.093, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.043-1.144) and attitude scores (OR = 1.255, 95% CI: 1.164-1.353) were associated with proactive practice; higher age was inversely associated (OR = 0.974, 95% CI: 0.950-0.998). SEM showed knowledge-attitude (β = 0.488, P = 0.001) and attitude-practice associations (β = 0.714, P = 0.001). The indirect knowledge-practice association through attitude was significant (β = 0.349, P = 0.001), whereas the direct path was not (β = 0.179, P = 0.064). Model fit and convergent-validity evidence were mixed. The surveyed caregivers reported limited knowledge but generally positive attitudes and proactive practices. The indirect statistical relationship through attitude does not establish causal mediation. Prospective studies are needed to validate the questionnaire further and evaluate caregiver-support interventions.

titre: Psychometric validation of domain-specific scores of the Oxford Cognitive Screen in patients with stroke.
auteurs: Iosa Marco, Morone Giovanni, Ciancarelli Irene, Demeyere Nele, Mancuso Mauro
revue: European journal of physical and rehabilitation medicine
resume: The Oxford Cognitive Screen (OCS) is a widely used tool for screening cognitive deficits in patients with stroke. It consists of 10 tests (yielding a total of 14 scores because two of the tests each generate three separate scores), covering six cognitive domains. However, using the OCS as an outcome measure requires standardized composite scores for each cognitive domain. The aim of this study is to psychometrically validate domain-specific composite scores derived from the OCS that are usable as outcome measures. Multicenter observational study. Inpatient and outpatient Rehabilitation Units. Data from 1973 patients with stroke and those of 498 healthy participants were considered. We developed formulas for combining the 14 test scores and computing a percentage score for each one of the six domains covered by the OCS (Executive functions, Language and arithmetic, Memory, Orientation, Visuomotor control, Spatial exploration). The discriminant and convergent validity of the proposed scores were tested by comparing data from patients with stroke and those of healthy participants, and by correlating these scores with those of the relevant domains of other clinical scales (NIH-Stroke Severity scale and Functional Independence Measure, FIM), respectively. Cronbach's alpha was used to test the reliability of these scores. The sensitivity to change was assessed by comparing the scores before and after rehabilitation in a subgroup of 311 patients and computing Cohen's d as the effect size. All six scores were significantly lower in patients (79.5±17.2%) than in healthy subjects (96.1±4.6%, P<0.001). All of them were significantly correlated with the relevant scores of other scales (r>0.59, P<0.001), with the exception of the score related to executive functions. The mean of these OCS scores significantly improved after rehabilitation (pre: 74.4±17.8% vs. post: 80.6±14.7%, P<0.001, Cohen's d=0.534). The differences between patients and healthy subjects support the discriminant validity, whereas the correlations with other scale scores support the convergent validity. The latter was not significant only for the proposed score for executive functions, likely because it is the only score without a comparator based exactly on the same construct, but rather on a subdomain of it (FIM problem solving). Good reliability and sensitivity to change were also demonstrated. Our results showed that the developed percentage composite scores are valid and may be useful for clinical staff already using the OCS to also use it as an outcome score for assessing cognitive domain deficits.

titre: Low-BMI sarcopenic obesity in adults with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities: A body composition analysis using bioelectrical impedance analysis and CT.
auteurs: Kohji Toshihiko, Takaiwa Miki, Ishida Akihiro, Naito Kiyoshi, Mori Hidehiko
resume: To clarify the prevalence, longitudinal changes, and body composition characteristics of sarcopenic obesity (SO) in institutionalized adults with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities (PIMD) using bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) and CT. From 101 screened residents, 77 institutionalized adults with PIMD (median age, 52 years) underwent annual BIA over three years. Sarcopenia was defined according to the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia 2019 criteria. Obesity was defined using body fat percentage thresholds (men ≥27%, women ≥38%). CT scans were available for 64 participants, including 31 with concurrent BIA. Factors associated with SO were examined using multivariable logistic regression. Sarcopenia was universal, and 51% exhibited SO. The SO group showed an "anthropometric paradox": higher BMI (18.2 vs. 15.9 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) but lower skeletal muscle index (SMI; 3.4 vs. 4.2 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) and phase angle (PA; 3.5 vs. 3.8°) than the sarcopenia-only group. Postural control ability (OR 0.38), SMI (OR 0.53), and PA (OR 0.41) were independently associated with SO. Over three years, SMI decreased (3.9 to 3.6 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) and body fat increased (31% to 35%) significantly. BIA markers demonstrated high concurrent validity; fat mass correlated with CT-measured total fat area (ρ = 0.84) and visceral fat area (ρ = 0.71), SMI with total abdominal muscle area (ρ = 0.778), and PA with low-attenuation muscle area (ρ = -0.501). BMI-based assessment alone underestimates adverse body composition in adults with PIMD. BIA and CT are valuable for detecting low-BMI SO and visualizing myosteatosis, supporting individualized nutritional and rehabilitation strategies.

titre: Concurrent Validity of Isokinetic Hip and Knee Strength Measurements Using the UGO Exoskeleton in Healthy Young Adults: Cross-Sectional Validation Study.
auteurs: Xie Hao, Ding Ming-Hui, Chen Pei-Ming, Ng Shamay S M, Wang Chu-Huai, Zhao Jiang-Li
resume: The UGO lower limb exoskeleton rehabilitation robot is designed for patients with lower limb motor dysfunction, and it can be used to assess the peak torque of hip and knee flexors and extensors. The primary aim of this study was to establish the concurrent validity of peak isokinetic torque using the UGO exoskeleton and Humac Norm dynamometers in healthy young adults. Twenty healthy young adults were enrolled in this study. All participants underwent isokinetic muscle strength tests using both the UGO exoskeleton and the Humac Norm dynamometers. Peak torque (Nm) of the hip and knee flexors and extensors was measured. The Pearson correlation coefficient was used to determine concurrent validity. Bland-Altman analysis was used to assess the agreement between the 2 devices. At the knee, peak torque of the extensors measured by the UGO exoskeleton correlated strongly with that measured by the Humac Norm dynamometer (right: r=0.662; P=.001; left: r=0.768; P<.001), with 95% limits of agreement (LoA) ranging from -22.89 to 82.21 Nm and from -24.60 to 75.65 Nm, respectively; the right knee flexors showed a moderate correlation (r=0.547; P=.01), with 95% LoA ranging from -26.27 to 36.01 Nm, whereas the left knee flexors showed no significant association (r=0.347; P=.12), with 95% LoA ranging from -2.40 to 75.02 Nm. At the hip, peak torque of the flexors correlated strongly on the right (r=0.615; P=.003) and moderately on the left (r=0.443; P=.04), with 95% LoA ranging from -15.52 to 86.57 Nm and from -12.53 to 98.50 Nm, respectively, whereas the bilateral hip extensors showed no significant association (right: r=0.337; P=.14; left: r=0.391; P=.20), with 95% LoA ranging from -51.57 to 76.80 Nm and from -28.19 to 79.59 Nm, respectively. In healthy young adults, the UGO exoskeleton demonstrated moderate to strong concurrent validity for peak torque of the bilateral knee extensors and hip flexors, but not for the nondominant knee flexors or bilateral hip extensors. The device may serve as a convenient torque assessment tool for selected muscle actions, but systematic overestimation and posture-related differences must be considered, and validation in the intended clinical population of patients with neurological conditions is required in further studies.

titre: Cross-cultural adaptation and reliability, agreement, and construct validity of the Turkish neck disability 10 in patients with neck pain.
auteurs: Tonak Hasan Atacan, Baştürk Sultan, Kırteke Duman Fatoş, Demirci Ozan
resume: To cross-culturally adapt the Neck Disability 10 (ND10) into Turkish and evaluate its measurement properties in adults with neck pain and related disorders. Following forward-backward translation, expert committee review, and cognitive debriefing, 200 Turkish-speaking adults with clinician-confirmed neck pain or neck-related disorders completed the ND10-TR, Neck Disability Index (NDI), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire (DASH), and American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons Shoulder Assessment Form (ASES). Eighty stable participants completed a 7-day retest. Structural validity, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, agreement, floor/ceiling effects, construct validity, and known-groups validity were examined. Cognitive debriefing supported comprehensibility, relevance, and comprehensiveness. Structural validity supported a one-factor solution, and internal consistency was excellent (Cronbach's α = 0.987; McDonald's ω = 0.992; ordinal α = 0.992). No floor/ceiling effects were observed. Test-retest reliability was excellent (ICC(2,1) = 0.952), with SEM = 5.61 and MDC95 = 15.54 points. Construct validity was supported by correlations with NDI (rₛ = 0.826), DASH (rₛ = 0.814), and ASES (rₛ = -0.768), and by known-groups validity across NDI categories. The ND10-TR is a comprehensible, reliable, and valid measure of neck-related functional disability for Turkish-speaking adults with neck pain, supporting rehabilitation assessment and outcome monitoring.

titre: Development and validation of a Chinese self-management ability assessment scale for patients with spinal cord injury.
auteurs: Li Jing, Wang Xin, Wang Xue-Yun, Li Hang, Hu Ya-Qin, Bao Ling-Yan, Chen Mei-Fen
resume: To develop and validate a scale for assessing self-management ability tailored for patients with spinal cord injury (SCI). The theoretical framework for the scale was the Integrated Theory of Health Behavior Change as well as the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health. The initial version of the scale was developed through literature review, qualitative interviews, and the Delphi expert consensus method. A total of 295 patients with SCI participated in the reliability and validity testing. The final scale consisted of 45 items across 5 dimensions: disease knowledge management, information and resource management, social-psychological management, daily behavior management, and rehabilitation exercise. The 5 dimensions displayed high reliability, with Cronbach's α values of 0.845-0.974, test-retest reliabilities of 0.718-0.94 and split-half reliabilities of 0.892-0.96. The content validity index was 0.961. Exploratory factor analysis identified five common factors, accounting for 66.105% of the cumulative variance. The self-management ability assessment scale for patients with SCI that was developed in this study was found to have acceptable reliability and validity and could effectively evaluate the self-management ability capacity of patients with SCI.

titre: Cross-cultural translation and psychometric validation of the Arabic Intermittent Catheterization Adherence Scale (ICAS): a bicentric study.
auteurs: El Feni Nedra, Heni Ines, Ghanmi Marwa, Gaddour Mariam, Mtaoua Sahbi, Alsaeed Mohammed Issa, Barakat Lolwa, Ceylan Halil Ibrahim, Stefanica Valentina, Dergaa Ismail
resume: Clean intermittent self-catheterization (CISC) is the reference treatment for neurogenic and non-neurogenic voiding dysfunction, yet adherence falls over time. The Intermittent Catheterization Adherence Scale (ICAS) measures this adherence, but no Arabic version has existed. We translated the ICAS into Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and tested its psychometric properties in 84 Tunisian adults on CISC at 2 rehabilitation departments. Translation followed forward and back translation guidelines, with a 6-member expert committee and a pretest of 20 patients. We assessed content validity with the content validity index (CVI), structure with exploratory factor analysis (EFA), internal consistency with Cronbach's alpha, and 10-day test-retest reliability with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The mean total score was 3.12 ± 2.03 on the 0 to 8 scale, with no floor or ceiling effect. Content validity was strong (scale-level CVI by averaging 0.99). The correlation matrix was suitable for factor analysis (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin 0.780; Bartlett p < 0.001). Parallel analysis supported a single factor explaining 40.1% of the variance, on which item 5 loaded weakly (0.25). Internal consistency was acceptable (alpha 0.75) and test-retest reliability excellent (single-measures ICC 0.97, 95% CI 0.95-0.98). Associations with clinical indicators were weak and non-significant. The Arabic ICAS reads best as a single-dimension screening measure for Tunisian patients and needs confirmation in larger, independent Arabic-speaking cohorts.

titre: Decision-centered wearable biosensors for personalized rehabilitation: integrating multimodal monitoring, artificial intelligence, and closed-loop intervention.
auteurs: Jia Fujin, Li Xinzhu, Song Hui, Liu Xinyue, Tang Yuli, Wen Qingping, Wu Ping
resume: Personalized rehabilitation requires repeated assessment of movement, physiological tolerance, fatigue, and adherence, yet conventional clinic-based measurements provide only intermittent snapshots. The convergence of wearable biosensors with artificial intelligence, edge-cloud computing, and connected data infrastructures creates an opportunity to convert continuous multimodal signals into timely rehabilitation decisions. This critical narrative review synthesizes physiological, biochemical, electrophysiological, biomechanical, and behavioral sensing within a monitoring-interpretation-feedback-adaptation-outcome framework. We first evaluate analytical validity, real-world robustness, biocompatibility, wearability, calibration drift, and power continuity. We then examine signal-quality control, multimodal fusion, digital biomarkers, federated learning, digital twins, and predictive models according to latency, uncertainty, generalizability, privacy, and decision utility. The review follows biosensor-derived information across a graded spectrum of action, from clinician-reviewed monitoring and real-time biofeedback to assist-as-needed adaptation, functional electrical stimulation, and state-responsive neuromodulation. Applications include motor and physiological assessment, fatigue-aware dose adjustment, musculoskeletal and neurological rehabilitation, posture correction, sensor-rich prosthetics, and Internet of Things-enabled home rehabilitation. Across these settings, greater autonomy increases the evidence and safety requirements: models should expose confidence, systems should degrade safely when signal quality falls, and digital infrastructures should preserve interoperability, version traceability, privacy, and accountable clinician oversight. The central translational gap is not sensor sensitivity alone but whether an integrated biosensor system produces a reliable metric, supports an explicit and proportionate decision, and improves an outcome important to the patient. Decision-centered evaluation can help move wearable biosensing from fragmented technology demonstrations toward secure, personalized, continuous, and clinically accountable rehabilitation.

titre: Rethinking neurophysiology of delayed onset muscle soreness: updated concepts and mechanisms for mitigation across endurance, resistance, and plyometric exercise.
auteurs: Jemni Monèm, Quodling Nicole, Hammami Nadhir, Groves Shad, Ijaz Azka, Pulyanova Daria, Hoffman Norman H, Bottoms Lindsay, Carrick Frederick R, Gu Yaodong
revue: Frontiers in sports and active living
resume: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is a physiological response to intense eccentric exercise across endurance, resistance, and plyometric training. Although traditionally attributed primarily to structural muscle damage and inflammation, accumulating evidence indicates that DOMS is a multifactorial neurophysiological response involving complex interactions between peripheral tissue responses, inflammatory signalling, neural sensitisation, proprioceptive alterations, and central nervous system adaptations. This review aimed to synthesise current evidence on the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying DOMS across endurance, resistance, and plyometric exercise within an integrated neurophysiological framework. It further examined the mechanisms underpinning therapeutic interventions, critically evaluated current approaches to DOMS assessment, and explored their implications for personalised recovery strategies, providing key-take-home to help clinicians and field partitioners. This systematic review with narrative synthesis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). 1,183 articles, including clinical trials examining DOMS neurophysiology and therapeutic interventions across exercise modalities were screened. The evidence indicates that DOMS cannot be explained by a single biological mechanism. Rather, distinct exercise modalities activate overlapping but different combinations of inflammatory, neural, metabolic, and proprioceptive pathways that influence symptom development and recovery. The findings further indicate that different exercise modalities elicit unique neuromuscular adaptations, with endurance training leading to cumulative inflammatory responses, resistance training inducing nociceptor sensitization, and plyometric exercise disrupting proprioceptive control. Endurance exercise produces IL-6 increase within 48 h but shows inflammation reduction after repeated bouts. Resistance training causes strength loss with Group III/IV nociceptor activation. Plyometric exercise disrupts proprioception alongside C-fiber sensitization. Recovery interventions show DOMS reduction: compression garments SMD = -0.44, acupuncture SMD = -0.89, foam rolling SMD = -0.34, but majority of studies lack extractable effect sizes preventing meta-analysis. Intervention efficacy appeared to vary according to exercise modality, exercise load, and individual neurophysiological responses, suggesting a dose-response influence on recovery outcomes. Collectively, the evidence supports the concept that DOMS should be regarded as a multifactorial neurophysiological response rather than simply a consequence of muscle damage. Exercise-specific recovery optimizes DOMS management: active recovery for endurance, compression/photobiomodulation for resistance, foam rolling/acupuncture for plyometric. Chronic training reduces DOMS through repeated bout adaptation. Future research should prioritise standardised outcome reporting together with mechanistic biomarkers and adequately designed longitudinal studies to strengthen the evidence base. This review highlights the need for individualized and exercise-specific recovery strategies to optimize DOMS mitigation, post-exercise recovery, and requires rehabilitation protocols based on neural and biochemical markers. Recovery interventions should also consider the dose-response relationship between exercise load and neurophysiological stress, as treatment effectiveness may vary according to DOMS severity and training demands. Given the variability in individual responses, integrating multiple assessment tools enhances accuracy and reliability in both research and clinical settings. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261294291, PROSPERO CRD420261294291.

titre: Markerless motion capture to quantify disability and functional performance in spine patients: a concurrent validity study bridging laboratory biomechanics and clinical practice.
auteurs: Haddas Ram, Shu Ye, Romiyo Prasanth, Ramirez Gabriel, Rubery Paul, Puvanesarajah Varun
revue: European spine journal : official publication of the European Spine Society, the European Spinal Deformity Society, and the European Section of the Cervical Spine Research Society
resume: Objective assessment of functional mobility is helpful in evaluating disability and treatment outcomes in patients with degenerative spine disease. Traditional marker-based motion capture offers laboratory-grade accuracy but is limited by complex setup, soft-tissue artifact, and practical challenges in clinical settings. Consequently, there is a gap in scalable, accurate, and clinically feasible methods to objectively assess spine-related functional performance in real-world settings. Markerless motion capture, powered by computer vision and deep-learning algorithms, enables marker-free, rapid, and reproducible assessment of three-dimensional kinematics in clinic settings. To evaluate the concurrent validity of a markerless motion capture system relative to a widely accepted reference method (marker-based motion capture) during gait and balance tasks in patients with spine pathology. A total of 116 participants (93 spine patients, 23 healthy controls) performed standardized gait and balance tasks captured simultaneously by marker-based and markerless systems. Agreement was examined using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman analysis, root mean square deviation (RMSD), and Pearson correlation. Across 580 gait and 348 balance trials, markerless motion capture demonstrated good to excellent agreement (ICC > 0.75) for trunk, lumbar, pelvic, and lower-extremity kinematics, with RMSD values ≤ 5°. Dynamic sagittal vertical axis (SVA) exhibited excellent reliability (ICC = 0.90, 95% CI: 0.84-0.94). Bland-Altman analysis showed minimal systematic bias. Balance assessments revealed excellent agreement for head sway in sagittal and coronal planes (ICC ≥ 0.97). However, transverse-plane rotations at the hip, knee, and ankle demonstrated poor agreement (ICC < 0.50), indicating current limitations for these specific parameters. Markerless motion capture provides quantifiable, accurate, and clinically applicable measures of spine-related movement. Its efficiency, scalability, and accuracy support objective evaluation of disability, enable individualized rehabilitation, and facilitate longitudinal outcome monitoring, highlighting its potential for integration into standard clinical workflows and bridging the gap between laboratory-grade biomechanics and routine spine care.

titre: Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Facial Palsy: A Narrative Review Across the Care Continuum.
auteurs: Elsherbini Adham, Perlmutter Jonah, Durowoju Ibrahim, Mosa Adam
resume: Facial paralysis produces substantial functional and psychosocial impairment which facial reanimation surgery seeks to mitigate by restoring facial movement and improving symmetry. However, despite technical advances in nerve- and muscle-based reconstruction, perioperative evaluation and outcome assessment remain largely subjective and variably reproducible. Artificial intelligence (AI) and computer vision have emerged as tools to provide objective, scalable assessment across the facial reanimation care pathway. MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched extensively to identify studies evaluating AI applications relevant to facial reanimation surgery. Included studies were screened by three independent reviewers and mapped to stages of perioperative care using an evidence-mapping framework. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria and were distributed across multiple stages of care. Evidence was most concentrated in diagnosis and severity assessment and in postoperative follow-up, where AI systems automated facial grading scales, quantified asymmetry, and extracted dynamic motion features from photographs and video. Several machine learning and deep learning models demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and strong correlations with clinician-assigned scores, often exceeding inter-rater reliability of traditional grading systems. Fewer studies addressed prognostic modeling, preoperative planning, or rehabilitation, though emerging applications included outcome prediction, three-dimensional symmetry analysis, and AI-assisted evaluation of spontaneous emotional expression after reanimation. AI applications in facial paralysis care are most mature in assessment and outcome measurement, where they offer improved objectivity and reproducibility. However, broader clinical integration will require larger, diverse datasets, prospective validation, and alignment with ethical and regulatory standards to demonstrate meaningful patient centered benefit.

titre: Reliability and Validity of AI-Based Pose Estimation Algorithms for Assessing Lower-Limb Flexibility and Joint Range of Motion.
auteurs: Okuno Hinata, Ishida Tomoya, Koshino Yuta, Kasahara Satoshi, Tohyama Harukazu, Samukawa Mina
resume: Muscle flexibility and joint range of motion (ROM) evaluation are essential for injury prevention and rehabilitation; however, conventional manual methods are limited in large-scale screening and self-monitoring because of examiner dependency and time constraints. This study evaluated the reliability and validity of AI-based pose estimation for lower-limb flexibility and ROM tests compared with conventional manual measurements. Twenty healthy volunteers (40 lower limbs; age 24.4 ± 2.6 years) underwent three flexibility tests-the Active Knee Extension Test (AKET), Modified Thomas Test (MTT), and Weight-Bearing Lunge Test (WBLT). The tests were assessed by a physiotherapist and three pose-estimation models (MediaPipe, OpenPose, and HRNet). Intra-rater reliability was evaluated with ICC(3,1). Concurrent validity and agreement were assessed using linear regression and Bland-Altman analysis. Intra-rater reliability was good to excellent for all methods (ICC ≥ 0.87), and concurrent validity was high (r<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0.80), except for MTT using the HRNet (r<sup>2</sup> = 0.73). Fixed biases were observed during the flexibility test. The limits of agreement ranged from ±8.04-10.87 cm for the AKET and MTT, and ±3.13-4.42 cm for WBLT. The WBLT showed a significant systematic bias, with an underestimation of -6.25° to -7.17° across all models. In young, healthy volunteers under standardized laboratory conditions, pose estimation models showed robust reliability and concurrent validity as objective tools for lower-limb flexibility assessment. However, systematic biases warrant caution regarding the interchangeability between AI-based measurements and conventional methods.

titre: Psychometric properties of the German Self-efficacy Expectation Scale (SES-G) in patients undergoing primary total hip arthroplasty: A validation study.
auteurs: Mooiweer Yvet, Danner Lena D, van den Akker-Scheek Inge, Linngrön Laura-Lee, Seeber Gesine H, Stevens Martin
revue: Zeitschrift fur Evidenz, Fortbildung und Qualitat im Gesundheitswesen
resume: To translate and culturally adapt the Self-efficacy Expectation Scale (SES) into German and examine its psychometric properties for total hip arthroplasty (THA) patients. The English-language SES was translated into German (SES-G). 116 patients completed the SES-G together with the Self-Efficacy for Rehabilitation Outcome Scale-German version (SER-G), Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Scale (HOOS), and Hospital for Special Surgery Hip Expectation Survey (HSS-HRES). Structural validity was assessed using an exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Construct validity was examined by testing predefined hypotheses on relationships between the SES-G and total- and subscores of the SER-G, HOOS, HSS-HRES. The SES-G was readministered after two weeks to assess test-retest reliability. To evaluate test-retest reliability 2-way random-effects absolute agreement intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analysis were calculated. MacDonald's Omega was used to evaluate internal consistency. Standard error of measurement (SEM) and minimal detectable change (MDC) were explored. EFA revealed three components explaining 75% of the total variance. For construct validity, 80% of the hypotheses were confirmed. Internal consistency was good (MacDonald's Omega = 0.81), as was test-retest reliability (ICC 0.71). Mean difference between the first and second administrations was -1.6 ± 4.2. The corresponding 95% CI did not contain zero [-2.4, -0.8], indicating systematic bias. Limits of agreement were 6.7 and 9.8. Proportional bias can be ruled out (B = 0.187, p = 0.05). SEM was 3.08, MDC<sub>ind</sub> and MDC<sub>group</sub> were 5.95 and 0.55, respectively. The psychometric analysis provides preliminary evidence that the SES-G is a valid and reliable instrument to measure self-efficacy in THA patients.

titre: Measurement Properties of the European Portuguese Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire (MHQ) in Paper and Electronic Formats: Instrument Validation Study.
auteurs: Moita Gonçalves Eugénio, Silva Maria Catarina, Ribeiro Henrique, Almeida Mariana, Filipe Bernardo, Branco Sandra, Henriques Filipa, Campos Lilibeth, Campolargo Ana, Cantista Pedro, Bernardes Miguel, Jácome Cristina
resume: The Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire (MHQ) is a key instrument for assessing hand and wrist conditions, but a validated version for European Portuguese speakers is unavailable. Furthermore, the potential of an electronic format to improve data collection and clinical workflows has not been formally evaluated. This study aimed to translate and culturally adapt the MHQ for European Portuguese and to evaluate the measurement properties and comparability of its paper and electronic formats. An observational study was conducted in three phases: (1) translation and expert review, (2) content validation through cognitive interviews, and (3) psychometric evaluation in a cohort of 81 adult patients with hand or wrist conditions. Exploratory known-groups analyses were performed according to clinical, sociodemographic, and digital-access variables. Analysis also included internal consistency (Cronbach α and McDonald ω), measurement error (standard error of measurement [SEM]), relative and absolute reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC], Spearman correlation coefficient [ρ], and Bland-Altman analysis). The electronic format's usability was assessed with the System Usability Scale (SUS). The translation and cognitive interviews confirmed the content validity and conceptual equivalence of the European Portuguese MHQ. The instrument demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach α=0.85-0.98; McDonald ω=0.88-0.99). Exploratory known-groups analyses showed significant gender-related differences and suggested side-specific clinical discrimination in fracture cases. While group-level relative reliability between formats was strong (ρ=0.68-0.91; ICC=0.76-0.95), individual-level absolute reliability was poor, with wide 95% limits of agreement spanning a 32.83-point interval. Format-related score discrepancies were most pronounced among older participants, those with lower educational attainment, and those with low digital literacy. The electronic MHQ was the preferred format (43 out of 74, 58%), showed acceptable usability (median SUS score 70, IQR 66-88), and had lower SEM in pain and function domains. The European Portuguese MHQ is a relevant and reliable instrument with adequate measurement properties for both clinical practice and research. The electronic version demonstrated superior precision and user preference. However, maintaining the paper format as a viable alternative is essential to ensure equitable access for patients with digital barriers. Due to the overall low absolute reliability between formats, once a patient-preferred format is adopted, it should be used consistently for longitudinal patient monitoring.

titre: Factors associated with drug-resistant epilepsy in children with epilepsy: a retrospective cohort study.
auteurs: Su Qunyan, Yin Yandan, Cheng Haiying, Yan Yinghua, Jin Jingjing, Shao Yiping, Sheng Jiangyin, Tao Anqian, Ruan Guiying, Cui Licheng, Feng Jianhua
resume: Drug‑resistant epilepsy (DRE) remains a major clinical challenge in children. Understanding clinical factors associated with drug resistance is important for guiding management. We aimed to investigate factors independently associated with DRE in a large cohort of children with epilepsy. A retrospective cohort study was conducted on children with confirmed epilepsy who received regular follow‑up at two tertiary pediatric epilepsy centers. Patients were classified into DRE [failure of ≥2 adequate anti-seizure medications (ASMs) trials] and non‑DRE groups according to ILAE criteria. Baseline demographic, clinical, electroencephalographic, neuroimaging, and treatment‑related variables were collected. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with DRE. Treatment‑related variables (number of ASMs tried, maximum concurrent ASMs, and polytherapy at last follow‑up) were excluded from the multivariable model due to their intrinsic relationship with the definition and clinical consequences of DRE. Model discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), and calibration was assessed by the Hosmer‑Lemeshow test. The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for performance metrics were obtained via bootstrap resampling. A total of 412 children were enrolled, including 100 (24.3%) with DRE. Children with DRE had significantly younger age at onset (4.30±3.40 vs. 6.01±3.50 years, P<0.001), higher baseline seizure frequency, more frequent status epilepticus, neurodevelopmental disorders, and psychiatric comorbidities (all P<0.05). In multivariable analysis excluding treatment‑related variables, generalized seizure type (vs. focal) [adjusted odds ratio (OR) =0.20; 95% CI: 0.04-0.62; P=0.01), history of status epilepticus (adjusted OR =4.86; 95% CI: 2.15-11.13; P<0.001), neurodevelopmental disorder (adjusted OR =3.40; 95% CI: 1.49-7.85; P=0.004), structural etiology (vs. genetic) (adjusted OR =0.25; 95% CI: 0.07-0.92; P=0.040), and older age at onset (adjusted OR =0.91; 95% CI: 0.82-1.00; P=0.046) were independently associated with DRE. The model showed moderate discriminative ability (AUC =0.802; 95% CI: 0.751-0.872). In this retrospective cohort, seizure type, history of status epilepticus, neurodevelopmental disorder, structural etiology, and older age at onset were independently associated with DRE after excluding treatment‑related variables. These findings suggest that true baseline independently associated variables of DRE are limited, and the diagnosis of DRE itself-failure of two adequate ASM trials-remains the most practical indicator for considering non‑pharmacological therapies. External validation is needed before clinical application.

titre: Screen time and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
auteurs: Zhao Caihong, Xu Jing, Wu Xirui, Li Yufen
resume: Children's exposure to electronic screens has risen sharply. This study quantitatively evaluated the association between excessive screen time and childhood attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) risk through a systematic review and meta-analysis, exploring the moderating roles of age and media type. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched observational studies assessing children's screen time and ADHD, and finally included 10 observational studies with overall low-to-moderate risk of bias. Risk of bias was evaluated using the ROBINS-I tool. Continuous data were unified using the Chinn conversion rule. A DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model calculated pooled odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Subgroup analyses, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, and Begg's and Egger's tests were also conducted. Excessive screen time was significantly associated with elevated childhood ADHD risk (pooled OR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.31-1.87, P < 0.001). Substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed (Q = 344.51, I2 = 97.4%, P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses revealed significant age-related heterogeneity: preschoolers (0-6 years) showed a larger magnitude of association (OR = 2.40, 95% CI: 1.44-3.98), whereas the association in school-age children and adolescents (>6 years) was of smaller magnitude (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05-1.29). Passive TV/video viewing showed a higher point estimate of ADHD risk (OR = 2.20) than interactive digital media (OR = 1.10), but the between-group difference did not reach statistical significance. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings. Excessive screen exposure is significantly associated with elevated ADHD risk in children, with distinct age-specific and media type-specific patterns. The preschool period appears to be a high-risk window for screen-related neurodevelopmental effects, with a trend toward stronger association for passive screen exposure. Public health and clinical interventions should prioritize restricting early screen exposure, particularly passive, fast-paced videos without substantial interaction.

titre: Genetic variants in NEF2L2 rs35652124 and GABRB3 rs2081648 genes: association with autism spectrum disorder in Iraqi children.
auteurs: Burhan Zainab Mohammed, Hoidy Wisam Hindawi
resume: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder of complex etiology with substantial genetic contribution. Oxidative stress and GABAergic dysregulation are implicated in the pathophysiology of ASD. Both genetic variations in NEF2L2 (Nuclear factor (erythroid-derived 2)-like 2, an antioxidant regulator) and GABRB3 (GABRB3 encodes the GABA-A receptor β3 subunit) may increase susceptibility to ASD. This is the first study of the two genes in this field in the context of the Iraqi children. Because the NEF2L2 control genotype distribution deviated significantly from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (χ<sup>2</sup> = 50.05, P < 0.0001), the NEF2L2 CT-genotype association below is reported as provisional pending independent genotyping verification; stratified subgroup findings are reported after Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction.This case-control study engaged 90 Iraqi children. Both GABRB3 rs2081648 and NEF2L2 rs35652124 polymorphisms were genotyped using Tetra-ARMS-PCR. GABA and NRF2 were also evaluated both using serum and protein, involved in elements of the oxidative stress, and biomarkers were analyzed. This study also conducted both a haplotype and an epistatic analysis. In exploratory analysis, the NEF2L2 rs35652124 CT genotype showed an apparent association with increased ASD risk; however, because the NEF2L2 control genotype distribution deviated severely from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, this association is provisional and is not treated as a confirmed finding of this study. The GABRB3 rs2081648 CT genotype presented robust evidence of protection. The ASD group was found to have a significant decrease in both GABRB3 (43.8%) and NRF2 (43.7%) proteins. The combined biomarker panel for the ASD population was AUC = 0.834. The T-C haplotype presented the most pronounced risk (OR = 2.84, P = 0.003; FDR q = 0.012). The two-locus epistatic interaction (P = 0.028, based on 1,000 permutations) is preliminary pending a confirmatory 10,000-permutation analysis. The GABRB3 polymorphism and serum GABRB3/NRF2 biomarkers are associated with GABA-mediated impairments in ASD in Iraqi children; the NEF2L2 CT-genotype association remains exploratory pending independent genotyping verification.

titre: Genomic structural equation modeling of impulsivity and risk-taking traits reveals three latent factors associated with brain structure and development.
auteurs: Shishikura Mari, Liu Lang, Yu Eric, Zhu Rui, Vilar-Ribó Laura, Cupertino Renata B, Palmer Abraham A, Sanchez-Roige Sandra, Vainik Uku, Morys Filip, Gan-Or Ziv, Misic Bratislav, Dagher Alain
revue: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
resume: Impulsivity is a multifaceted transdiagnostic trait that emerges in childhood. Research has identified genetic loci and brain systems associated with different facets of impulsivity and risk-taking. However, how these genetic underpinnings overlap across different facets, and how they are associated with brain development during childhood remain unknown. Using genomic structural equation modeling on 17 impulsivity and risk-taking traits, we identified latent factors capturing underlying genetic architecture. We then calculated polygenic scores for these factors using Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study data (N = 4,142) and examined their associations with brain structure, development, and behavior in children aged 9-14 years. Finally, we tested whether socioeconomic status modulated the associations between latent polygenic scores and brain structures. We identified three distinct genetic latent factors, which we label lack of self-control, reward drive, and sensation seeking. In children, polygenic scores for the three factors showed associations with partly differentiated brain patterns: lack of self-control associated with reduced prefrontal cortical thickness, reward drive with increased subcortical cellular density, and sensation seeking with increased cortical surface area and white matter integrity. Longitudinally, lack of self-control predicted variation in white matter development. We found little evidence that socioeconomic factors modulated associations between polygenic scores and brain structure. Using genome-wide association study data of European genetic ancestry samples, we identified three genetically distinct dimensions of impulsivity and risk-taking. These genetic predispositions showed association with brain structure as early as ages 9-10, with limited evidence that these associations varied across socioeconomic context.

titre: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome Following Three Randomized Controlled Trials of Choline in Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD).
auteurs: Wozniak Jeffrey R, Eckerle Judith K, Gimbel Blake A, Ernst Abigail M, Anthony Mary E, Tuominen Kent A, de Water Erik, Doughty Alexandra L, Zeisel Steven H, Georgieff Michael K
resume: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) represents a range of neurodevelopmental outcomes from prenatal alcohol exposure for which there are few interventions. Preclinical studies have identified choline as a potential treatment for cognitive deficits in FASD. We previously conducted three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in children under age 6 and reported on memory benefits following all three trials. Two RCTs compared a fixed 500 mg daily dose to placebo, and the third RCT tested a weight-adjusted choline dose. Here, we report on a longitudinal follow-up 5 years post-study completion. The RCTs included 2.5- to 5.9-year-old children with FASD who received choline (n = 53) or placebo (n = 51). Participants described here (n = 28 choline; n = 30 placebo) were 9.1 years old on average at follow-up. Of these, 9% had fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), 43% partial FAS (PFAS), and 48% alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ARND). Parents completed a diagnostic interview and behavior checklists while participants completed assessments of general cognitive ability, executive functioning, and memory. Participants who received choline in the initial RCT showed a medium effect size performance advantage (9.1% better) for non-verbal IQ and a medium effect size advantage (11.3% better) for working memory over placebo. Age at enrollment did not explain significant variance in outcome but choline dose was significantly associated with non-verbal IQ and working memory (higher dose contributed to better performance at follow-up). High rates of anxiety disorders and impulse-control disorders were observed. While there were no statistically significant differences in mental health diagnoses for choline versus placebo, there were some differences that neared significance. Very few RCTs have been conducted in FASD, and interventions targeting cognitive functioning are needed. The data reported here suggest that choline supplementation has long-lasting neurodevelopmental benefits, especially in non-verbal IQ and working memory for individuals with FASD.

titre: When sex matters early: clues from pediatric onset multiple sclerosis.
auteurs: Lorefice Lorena, Zivadinov Robert
resume: Pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis (POMS) provides a unique developmental model to investigate when sex differences first emerge in multiple sclerosis (MS). As disease onset occurs during immune, endocrine, and neural maturation, POMS offers an opportunity to understand how puberty may shape disease susceptibility and subsequent trajectories. This review synthesizes evidence from epidemiological, clinical, neuroimaging, biomarker, and therapeutic studies across prepubertal, peripubertal, and post-pubertal stages. Articles published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through a PubMed/MEDLINE search using terms related to POMS, sex differences, and puberty. Available data indicate that the transition from childhood to adolescence coincides with the emergence of female predominance and sex-dependent patterns of tissue injury. MRI, retinal imaging, and fluid biomarkers suggest that differences in neuroaxonal vulnerability may be detectable early in the disease course. However, most studies remain sex-agnostic. Sexual dimorphism in MS may emerge earlier than previously recognized, with puberty representing a critical window in which sex-related biological changes begin to shape disease susceptibility and expression. Incorporating sex and pubertal stage into longitudinal POMS research may help elucidate the mechanisms driving these differences, refine early risk stratification, and ultimately support more individualized therapeutic strategies across the MS lifespan.

titre: Home visits following hospital discharge for families with preterm and low-birthweight infants.
auteurs: Durao Solange, Gloeck Natasha R, Odendaal Willem A, Hohlfeld Ameer, Brand Amanda, Gordon Sarah, Balakrishna Yusentha, Kredo Tamara
revue: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
resume: Home visiting programmes are widely used to support families of preterm and low-birthweight (LBW) infants after hospital discharge, yet evidence on their effectiveness is limited and of variable quality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). A comprehensive, up-to-date review was needed to inform healthcare decisions. To assess the effectiveness of home visits following hospital discharge compared to standard of care or no home visits, for families/caregivers of preterm or LBW infants to reduce morbidity and mortality and enhance health and well-being. We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP, together with reference checking, to identify eligible studies. The latest search date was April 2026. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of preterm and LBW infants and their caregivers comparing home visits after discharge from hospital with no home visits or standard of care including home visits. There were no restrictions on language or publication status. Our critical outcomes included all-cause mortality, neurodevelopment, morbidity, growth, breastfeeding rates, exclusive breastfeeding, and emergency hospital visits. Important outcomes were hospital readmission rates, maternal/parental emotional well-being, and maternal-infant interaction. We used Cochrane's RoB 2 tool to assess the risk of bias. We synthesised results for each outcome in meta-analysis where possible, using random-effects models to calculate risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes, mean differences (MDs) or standardised mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes, and hazard ratios (HRs) for time-to-event outcomes, along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome. We included 35 RCTs, of which 28 (12,021 infants and 10,056 mothers/caregivers) contributed data to our prespecified outcomes. Most studies were from high-income countries; however, approximately 70% of participants were from a large study in India contributing data to comparison 2. The content, timing, duration, and frequency of home visits varied widely. Twenty-one studies contributed data to meta-analyses. Home visits versus no home visits The effects of home visits on all-cause mortality at one year are very uncertain (RR 3.08, 95% CI 0.13 to 73.27; 1 study, 79 participants). Home visits may have little to no effect on cognitive development (SMD 0.06, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.29; 3 studies, 287 participants), and likely have little to no effect on motor development (SMD -0.02, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.33; 1 study, 127 participants). The effect on morbidity, specifically on diarrhoea at six months, is very uncertain (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.19; 1 study, 179 participants). Home visits likely have little to no effect on growth, specifically weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ) at six months (MD -0.09, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.18; 1 study, 179 participants). Home visits likely increase the proportion of infants breastfeeding at six months (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.37; I² = 0%; 4 studies, 1217 participants) and may result in a large increase in exclusive breastfeeding at six months (RR 2.31, 95% CI 0.85 to 6.29; 3 studies, 1129 participants). The certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low due to risk of bias and imprecision. More intensive home visits versus less intensive home visits (part of standard of care) Home visits with community-initiated kangaroo mother care likely reduce all-cause mortality at 6 months (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.93; 1 study, 8402 participants), likely have little to no effect on cognitive (MD 0.21, 95% CI -1.77 to 2.19; 1 study, 552 participants) or motor development (MD -0.85 95% CI -2.59 to 0.89; 1 trial, 552 participants) at 12 months, and likely reduce morbidity, specifically rates of diarrhoea slightly at 3 months (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.04; 1 study, 7654 participants) and the risk of possible serious bacterial infections slightly at 28 days (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.97; 1 study, 8384 participants). They likely have little to no effect on WAZ at six months (MD -0.01, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.04; 1 study, 7086 participants) and likely reduce the proportion of infants who are severely underweight at six months slightly (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.04; 1 study, 6641 participants). More intensive home visits may have little to no effect on breastfeeding at six months (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.59; 1 study, 308 participants), and their effect on exclusive breastfeeding at six months is very uncertain (RR 1.97, 95% CI 0.19 to 20.62; I² = 84%; 3 studies, 7091 participants). The certainty of the evidence was moderate for all outcomes except for breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding, for which it was low and very low, respectively. The certainty of evidence was downgraded for risk of bias, imprecision, and indirectness. No study in either comparison reported on emergency hospital visits. Home visits likely improve breastfeeding and may improve exclusive breastfeeding compared to no home visits. They may have little to no effect on cognitive development, and likely have little to no effect on motor development or growth. The effects on mortality or diarrhoea are very uncertain. In places where home visits are already implemented, enhancing them so that they are more intensive than the standard of care (i.e. more frequent, longer, delivered by specialised personnel, with kangaroo mother care, etc.) likely reduces mortality, morbidity, and the risk of underweight. However, they likely have little to no effect on cognitive and motor development or WAZ, and may have little to no effect on breastfeeding rates. The effects on exclusive breastfeeding are very uncertain. Better-quality studies are needed, particularly in LMICs. There is a need for studies reporting on the critical outcome of emergency hospital visits, and to standardise outcome measures reported in this area of research, particularly for mental health and neurodevelopment outcomes. This review was conducted for the GELA project (africa.cochrane.org/projects/GELA) which is funded as part of the EDCTP2 programme (grant number RIA2020S-3303-GELA) supported by the European Union. Protocol: CRD42024496298 registered on 15 January 2024 (PROSPERO), available at https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024496298.

titre: Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging for preoperative evaluation of cerebral microstructure and neurodevelopment in children with congenital heart disease.
auteurs: Xu Shengfang, Zhang Jinlong, Wang Shaoyu, Qian Jifang, Zhu Dalin, Zhang Jing
revue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
resume: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a type of heart structure defect caused by the abnormal development of the heart and major blood vessels during the embryonic stage. With the continuous innovation of surgical treatment techniques and the improvement of perioperative management, the survival rate of children with CHD has significantly improved. However, accompanying central nervous system development problems have become increasingly prominent. This study investigated the clinical utility of neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) in evaluating preoperative cerebral microstructural features and neurodevelopmental status in children with CHD. Fifty-five infants with CHD were prospectively enrolled in the CHD group, and 55 age- and sex-comparable typically developing infants were included as the control group. All participants completed the Gesell Development Schedules assessment. The developmental quotient (DQ) and domain-specific subscale scores for five core developmental domains were recorded: adaptive behavior (AB), fine motor (FM), gross motor (GM), language (L), and personal-social behavior (PSB). Diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) was acquired in all participants, and multiparametric NODDI maps were generated on a postprocessing workstation (Siemens Healthineers). The derived quantitative parameters included extracellular volume fraction (ECVF), neurite density index (NDI), isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF), and the orientation dispersion index (ODI). Intergroup differences in NODDI parameters and Gesell developmental scores were statistically analyzed. Pearson product-moment correlation analysis was then applied to evaluate associations between region-specific NODDI parameters and individual Gesell domain scores within the CHD group. The ECVF in the splenium of the corpus callosum (SCC) of the CHD group was significantly lower than that of the control group (t=-2.261; P=0.026), whereas the ECVF in the frontal white matter (FWM) was significantly higher (t=2.242, P=0.027). ODI measurements in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (PLIC) were significantly lower in the CHD group than in the control group (t=2.401; P=0.018). Intracellular volume fraction (ICVF) values in the PLIC and SCC were also significantly higher in the CHD group (PLIC: t=4.489, P<0.001; SCC: t=2.388, P=0.019). ODI measurements in the occipital white matter (OWM) were significantly lower in the CHD group than in the control group (t=3.707; P<0.001). Compared to the control group, the CHD group had significantly lower ISOVF measurements in the PTR (t=-2.119, P=0.038), FWM (t=-2.825, P=0.006), OWM (t=-2.253; P=0.028), and temporal white matter (t=-2.164; P=0.034). Correlation analysis further showed that Gesell scores, including DQ, AB, FM, GM, L, and PSB, were consistently lower in the CHD group than in the control group. Within the CHD cohort, the NDI value of the PLIC showed a positive correlation with DQ, AB, FM, GM, L, and PSB, whereas the ODI value of the PLIC showed a positive correlation with PSB. The ISOVF value of the genu of the corpus callosum showed a positive correlation with DQ, AB, L, and PSB. The NDI value of the SCC showed a positive correlation with AB and L. NODDI sensitively detects preoperative cerebral microstructural changes in children with CHD, and its key parameters correlate with preoperative neurodevelopmental performance. Thus, NODDI-derived parameters may serve as candidate imaging biomarkers for evaluating brain microstructure and development before surgery, offering objective imaging-based support for early clinical assessment and timely intervention.

titre: The weight of junk food: Smaller hippocampal, amygdala, and prefrontal volumes in adolescents-The Cogni-Action Project.
auteurs: Cristi-Montero Carlos, Peña-Jorquera Humberto, Sanchez-Martinez Javier, Martin Gastón Pavez-San, Solis-Urra Patricio, Ferrari Gerson, López-Gil José Francisco
resume: Most studies investigating diet-brain relationships in youth focus on single foods. Whether the joint consumption of multiple food groups is associated with neuroanatomy during adolescence remains largely unexplored, particularly outside high-income countries. In this cross-sectional study, 61 Chilean adolescents (11.6 ± 1.07 years; 42.6% girls) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Volumes of total gray matter, hippocampus, amygdala, and selected prefrontal regions were extracted. Dietary intake was assessed using the Global Food Quality Index questionnaire. Confounder-adjusted linear regressions examined individual food group-brain associations, with correction for multiple comparisons. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) was used to identify multivariate food group-brain covariation with permutation-based inference. Univariate analyses showed a significant inverse association between pastry consumption and hippocampal volume (β = -0.402, 95% CI: -0.571 to -0.228, adjusted R<sup>2</sup> = 0.34). CCA identified one significant multivariate mode linking higher unhealthy food consumption to brain volumes (r = -0.70, p = .008). Pastries, fried foods, and soft drinks showed the strongest contributions, whereas the corresponding brain variate was characterized by smaller hippocampal, amygdala, and anterior cingulate/prefrontal volumes. In conclusion, higher consumption of unhealthy food groups is associated with smaller limbic-prefrontal volumes in adolescents. Although causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data, these findings highlight adolescence as a critical window for diet-brain health research.

titre: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
auteurs: Liu Yong, Wang Jiayuan, Duan Ruonan, Wang Xiaoyi, Zhang Jie, Li Mengru, Sun Jian, Zeng Yulin, Kan Haopeng, Meng Tonghui, Liu Xinrui, Zhang Yu, Tang Jiexin, Shi Kexin, Wei Ziyu, Jin Yecheng, Li Jiangxia, Li Xi, Liu Qiji, Ma Jinlong, Gao Yuan, Sun Wenjie
resume: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

titre: Early postnatal brain volumes and two-year cognitive outcomes in preterm infants: An exploratory machine learning study.
auteurs: Savvopoulos Fotios, de Munck Sophie, van den Bosch Gerbrich E, Bouw Nienke, Dudink Jeroen, Vermeulen Marijn J, Schnack Hugo G, Van Haren Neeltje E M
resume: Premature birth is associated with an increased risk of cognitive and motor developmental problems. Early prediction of these outcomes is crucial for timely intervention and adequate follow-up. This study aimed to predict cognitive and motor outcomes in preterm-born infants using brain volumetric features in combination with clinical and demographic perinatal characteristics, and to compare the performance of three different machine learning algorithms. We acquired quantitative structural brain MRI at approximately 30 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA) and clinical and demographic birth characteristics including gestational age, sex, birthweight, and maternal education level. Machine learning techniques were applied to predict cognitive (N = 63) and motor (N = 41) outcomes at two years corrected age, assessed using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development III, in infants born before 30 weeks gestation. We evaluated the performance of logistic regression, linear support vector classifier (linear SVC), and k-nearest neighbour (KNN). Employing volumetric features only, KNN achieved a validation accuracy of 0.64, showing modest predictive power for cognitive outcomes. Adding clinical characteristics did not significantly improve accuracy. The models did not perform better than chance when predicting motor outcomes. Volumetric features demonstrated modest predictive ability for cognitive outcomes, and the addition of clinical features did not significantly improve performance. The low to moderate overall validation accuracy underscores, however, the challenges faced in the clinical application of machine learning in neuroimaging. The reliability and clinical applicability of predictions of outcomes from advanced neuroimaging data will largely depend on the quantity and quality of the data, methodological standardisation, and the generalisability of the prediction models.

titre: Clinical practice guidelines for neonatal therapeutic hypothermia across European Society for Paediatric and Neonatal Intensive Care (ESPNIC) member countries: a multidisciplinary blind comparison.
auteurs: De Luca Daniele, Neri Costanza, Alonso-Ojembarrena Almudena, Ippolito Mariachiara, Milan Anna, Piastra Marco, Sanchez-Luna Manuel, Schettler Karl F, Zanin Anna, Ghi Tullio, Cortegiani Andrea
resume: Therapeutic hypothermia (TH) decreases mortality and neuro-developmental disability in neonates greater or equal than 36 weeks' gestation with moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) due to perinatal asphyxia. TH is often applied in different ways, as national guidelines and target populations may significantly differ. We aimed to compare TH guidelines from various European countries as we hypothesised that guidelines are significantly different and often of insufficient quality. Multidisciplinary, blind, critical appraisal of clinical practice guidelines using AGREE-II and RIGHT tools to assess their quality and completeness of the reporting, respectively. The appraisal was performed by neonatologists, obstetricians, paediatric and adult intensivists. The raters were kept unaware of the identity of the other panellists and each of them performed the evaluation of the guidelines independently. Total AGREE-II score was different amongst the guidelines (p = 0.008): the German guidelines scored highest (5.2 (95% CI: 4.7-5.7), while the others had comparable intermediate scores (approximately between 2.2 and 4.4). A good score in the rigour of development was not achieved by any guideline (German guidelines scored "moderate"). The overall completeness of reporting was different amongst the guidelines, with total completeness ranging between 20% and 49% (p < 0.0001). Completeness of reporting was incomplete for most rater-item responses. German and French guidelines had the best domain-based reporting completeness for AGREE-II and RIGHT, respectively. Inter-rater agreement was satisfactory (intraclass correlation coefficient varying between 0.83 and 0.91; p < 0.001). European guidelines for neonatal TH have a general insufficient quality and completeness of reporting. None.
